profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Smallest workload (1024 float16) and the strongest control for isolating host launch cost: the device kernel is one program, so any remaining time is per-call host work. Profiled at both metrics and instruction level.
Highest eval latency of the round; mid-size regime with an 8-program grid, used to check whether latency tracks device work at all.
Second-lowest speedup and the float16 member of the 1M regime where device time is non-trivial; completes the three-dtype 1M comparison.
Lowest speedup of the round and the largest device workload (128 programs, bfloat16 1M); primary case for the low-speedup regime.
float32 control at the smallest size: pairs with uniform-timing-0 to test whether dtype changes the small-input floor.
Highest speedup and the float32 member of the 1M regime; control showing that the same device shape yields the best score when the reference measured slow.

findings.label: Eval latency is flat across 1024 to 1M elements while the device kernel spans 2.8-26.5 us, so per-call host work dominates every workload

evidence.metric: Task Duration(us) of _uniform_kernel with Block Num=1 (1024 float16)
Task Duration(us) of _uniform_kernel with Block Num=1 (1024 float32)
Task Duration(us) of _uniform_kernel with Block Num=8 (65536 float16)
Task Duration(us) of _uniform_kernel with Block Num=128 (1048576 bfloat16)
operation_count per measured call (single device task, no copies)

findings.inference: Authoritative eval latencies from get_profile_context are 0.0979-0.1039 ms for all nine timing workloads, i.e. the 1M cases (98.3-102.8 us) are no slower than the 1024 cases (97.9-99.0 us) even though their device kernel is 9.5x larger (26.4 us vs 2.8 us). Because the same source issues exactly one `_uniform_kernel` device task per call and no auxiliary copies, the invariant ~98 us per call must be host-side: `torch.empty_like`, the `torch_device_fn.current_device()` query, the fresh `_rng_state` read, the three dict lookups and the Triton `_uniform_kernel[grid](*args)` dispatch. Fitting device time inside 98-104 us requires host >=~72-96 us on every workload, so the eval latency floor is set by submission, not by the kernel. Calibrated at high confidence because the flat-latency and single-task facts are direct measurements; the exact host split is not measurable with the capabilities advertised here.

findings.label: Device queue is starved between calls: ~98-135 us of task wait versus 2.8-26.5 us of kernel busy time

evidence.metric: Task Wait Time(us) of steady-state call (1024 float16)
inter-launch interval from Task Start Time(us) row3->row4 (1024 float16)
Task Wait Time(us) of steady-state call (65536 float16)
Task Wait Time(us) of steady-state call (1048576 bfloat16)

findings.inference: In the profiled run the device sits idle 98-135 us before each launch and launches arrive every ~106-148 us, so the AIV cores are busy only ~2% (1024) to ~20% (1M) of the submission cycle. This is queue starvation caused by the host producing work more slowly than the device consumes it, not a barrier or dependency inside the kernel. The profiled interval (~130-140 us) is larger than the eval latency (~98 us) because instrumentation adds overhead, so the two must not be subtracted; the qualitative ordering (device idle >> device busy) is what the artifact supports. Indirectly this also bounds any possible device-side gain: even an instantly-finished kernel could not move eval latency much while submission costs ~98 us.

findings.label: For 1M elements the kernel is vector-compute bound in the mixer, not memory bound: vec ratio ~0.83 versus MTE3 ~0.03 and MTE2 ~0

evidence.metric: aiv_vec_ratio
aiv_mte3_ratio
aiv_mte2_ratio
aiv_vec_time_us
aiv_mte3_ratio (float32 1M, 4 MiB store)

findings.inference: The 1M kernel spends 22.2-22.7 us in the vector pipe and only 0.76-1.15 us storing; the store grows with dtype width (2 MiB fp16/bf16 vs 4 MiB fp32) while vec time does not, which is the opposite of a bandwidth-limited kernel. Logical output traffic of 2 MiB in 26.4 us is ~80 GB/s of effective write throughput, far under the device's capability and explicitly not named as HBM utilization here because no matched physical-byte counter was read. So the mixer arithmetic (two 32-bit multiplies, three xor-shifts, the sign map and the clamp, plus conversion) is the device limit for this regime. Because the same kernel is only ~27% of the 98-104 us eval latency, this is a secondary opportunity today.

findings.label: In the generated instruction stream the sign map (main.py:90) and the interval clamp (main.py:93) dominate vector cost, and both expand into compare/select/mask plus BAR and flag traffic

evidence.metric: source hotspot cycles for main.py:93 (tl.minimum/tl.maximum clamp), 166 calls
source hotspot cycles for main.py:90 (tl.where sign map), 77 calls
mapped instructions / listed instructions
aiv_vec_time_us for the same profiled kernel

findings.inference: For a single 1024-element program the two source lines that implement the sign map and the interval clamp account for 0.92 us of the 1.194 us vector time under simulator scope, emitted as VCMPV/VSEL/MOVEMASK/VMOVMASK_XN/VNOT sequences bracketed by BAR, SET_FLAG and WAIT_FLAG. The mapping `xi<0 ? -xi-1 : xi` exists only to turn the signed word into a magnitude, and the clamp exists only to force the result back inside [lo,hi]; a bit-slice mapping (e.g. consuming the top bits of the mixed word) would remove the branch-and-select entirely, and the clamp is provably redundant whenever the host interval rounding already guarantees the value lands in range. Confidence is medium and scope is one 1024-element program: 616/641 instructions are source-mapped, simulator time is diagnostic only, and this listing was not collected for a 1M program, so the cycle share is not transferable as a measured speedup.

findings.label: The round-4 int32 counter fold removed the int64 device path: all three 1M dtypes run the kernel in 26.33-26.53 us with 32-bit vector instructions

evidence.metric: avg_duration_us of _uniform_kernel (1048576 float16)
avg_duration_us of _uniform_kernel (1048576 bfloat16)
avg_duration_us of _uniform_kernel (1048576 float32)
vector opcode width present in listing (VMULS/VAND/VSHR/VCONV, no 64-bit integer vector op)

findings.inference: The three 1M dtypes differ in output width by 2x yet agree on kernel duration within 0.2 us, which is what a 32-bit-lane arithmetic kernel with a negligible store would produce and is inconsistent with a promoted 64-bit path. Round 3 measured 0.746 ms on these same 1M cases; round 4 measures 98.3-102.8 us of eval latency and 26.3-26.5 us of device kernel, so the frozen hypothesis (fold the counter epoch into the key to keep seed/off below 2**31) is supported by these measurements. The instruction listing is from the 1024-element program, so the width claim is scoped there and combined with the dtype-invariance measurement rather than asserted on its own.

findings.label: The 0.891 and 0.947 low scores are reference-side measurement variance, not a slow candidate case

evidence.metric: min_duration_us / max_duration_us of _uniform_kernel across 100 invocations (1048576 bfloat16)
min_duration_us / max_duration_us of _uniform_kernel across 100 invocations (1048576 float16)

findings.inference: The two lowest-speedup workloads are the most device-stable ones (3% spread over 100 invocations) and their candidate eval latencies, 0.0983 and 0.1028 ms, sit inside the 0.0979-0.1039 ms band that the other seven workloads occupy. Their speedups are low because the reference side measured fast in those runs (0.0876 and 0.0974 ms) while the highest-speedup float32 1M case measured a slow 0.1089 ms reference with an almost identical candidate latency (0.0999 ms). So the residual spread of the round is reference-side jitter of roughly +-10%, and bfloat16 1M should not be treated as a defective kernel regime.

performance_interpretation: Round 4 passes with geo_mean 1.0254 (from 0.5048 at the round-2 baseline) and every timing workload between 0.891x and 1.090x, so the frozen int32 counter-fold hypothesis was correct and the round-3 int64 collapse is gone. The profiler shows why the score stops near 1.0 rather than climbing: the candidate's device work is now tiny (2.79 us at 1024, 7.61 us at 65536, 26.4 us at 1M) but its eval latency is pinned at 97.9-103.9 us for every size and dtype, and the per-call device queue shows 98-135 us of idle wait against 2.8-26.5 us of kernel busy time. The remaining cost is the host submission path of one Triton dispatch per call plus output allocation, device query, bounds/tile lookups and the host RNG counter. Because the reference implementation is also pinned in the same 87.6-108.9 us band with only ~5.5 us of device work in three tasks, the match is a tie between two host-bound implementations; beating it requires going below the ~98 us submission cost, not improving the kernel. Device-side headroom exists only in the 1M regime (26.4 us, vector-bound at ratio 0.83 with the sign map and clamp as the largest vector contributors) and would become relevant only after the host floor is cut.

next_experiment.action_description: Keep the counter-based RNG, interval rounding and kernel math exactly as in round 4 and change only the host submission path for the non-constant-interval branch: cache the compiled `_uniform_kernel` handle keyed by (dtype, BLOCK, EVEN, scalar types) and launch it directly on the current stream with the current output address, instead of calling the full `_uniform_kernel[grid](*args)` JIT dispatch on every call; in the same edit hoist the per-call `torch_device_fn.current_device()` query out of the hot path by caching the device index and revalidating it only when the output device differs. Read the current stream and current `out.data_ptr()` on every call, use a size()-bearing integer address wrapper so the profiling launcher still sees parameter metadata, and send the freshly advanced 31-bit counter exactly as today. Do not change the kernel body, the bounds computation, or the allocations in this round.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Eval latency should drop from ~98 us toward roughly 40-60 us on all nine timing workloads, because the profiler already shows only 2.8-26.5 us of device work per call. With the reference stuck at 87.6-108.9 us, headline geo_mean should rise from 1.0254 to roughly 1.8-2.5x; the 1M cases should improve by more in absolute terms only after the host floor falls below their 26.4 us of device work.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risk 1: the private FlagTree launcher ABI is fragile and the profiling launcher calls size() on parameters, which previously produced 'process exits without a completion marker'. Mitigation: keep the standard `kernel[grid](...)` path as the fallback and select it if the cached-handle launch raises; do not switch paths based on whether timing is active. Risk 2: a bind-then-execute wrapper that executes once during binding would submit twice. Mitigation: warm up/compile only, then execute exactly once, and verify one device task per call in the paired trace. Risk 3: caching keyed on shape could serve a stale address. Mitigation: the current data_ptr must be part of every launch and never cached. Rollback: revert to the round-4 source, SHA 7d89bcc126f65c289f29223af058f37a8238606361b7ccf324e710d3af07e646, which is already a valid 1.0254x delivery.
success_criteria: Full 36-item contract passes unchanged (9 correctness plus 9 timing), including fresh values on every call, new allocation per call, [from,to) upper-bound exclusion, the from==to fill branch, and the fp16/bf16/fp32 statistical and range gates.
All nine timing workloads measure below 80 us and at least 7 of 9 are >=20% below their round-4 latency (0.0979-0.1039 ms).
Headline geo_mean exceeds the round-4 value of 1.0254 with no workload below the round-4 floor of 0.891, and correctness status stays PASSED.

A paired device trace for the final source shows exactly one `_uniform_kernel` device task per call, no extra MEMCPY tasks, and the same 26.3-26.5 us kernel duration at 1M, confirming the gain came from the host path rather than from altered device work.

warnings: msprof and simulator timings are diagnostic only; every latency and speedup quoted comes from the authoritative round-4 eval.
The instruction listing covers only one 1024-element program (616/641 instructions source-mapped); its cycle shares must not be transferred to the 1M program or read as a measured speedup.
No Roofline figure is claimed: the ~80 GB/s effective write throughput is logical bytes over measured kernel time, not a matched physical HBM counter, and no hardware ceiling was calibrated.
All profiling was on physical card 7 / npu:0 only; nothing here validates multi-device behavior.
open_questions: How the ~98 us per-call budget splits between `torch.empty_like`, the device query, the host RNG state read and the Triton dispatch itself, since no host-side timing capability is advertised by the service.

Whether the 1M vector cost would matter once the host floor is removed; the sign map and clamp removal is a plausible follow-up but its benefit is untested and currently capped at ~10 us of a 98 us call.
Whether a direct-handle launch will clear the ~98 us floor at all, given that a cached-call attempt in an earlier round of this campaign passed correctness without improving performance.
